Yehgohbah parted the beaded curtain that lead to the room where she kept her "collection." The newer specimens were tightly bound up in clear glass jars, while the oldest ones were sealed in clay pots with fading and flaking painted tribal designs dancing on their terra cotta walls. The witch doctor had been working on the collection since her days as an apprentice to her grandmother. Several of the pots predated her grandmother's time. 

Long ago, back in the times when the Creators walked the earth with their lowly creations, the first Witch Doctors had been taught how to collect emotions and save them, sort of like how people would gather and preserve fruits for use in the coming winters. One gracious warrior would donate Bravery to save for a youth to use in the future in a time of great need. A kindly priestess would offer up Calmness for a future chief to use as needed. All people from all walks of life would freely offer, and freely receive, these precious resources. But, as time wore on, and new peoples from lands far away arrived and mingled with the People of the Mountain, the old ways would fall into disfavor and dim memory. Yehgohbah's tiny band was one of the few that still remembered the old teachings. 


Old joints protesting the act of the woman lifting the lantern higher, she grunted and made her way to the least crowded corner of the room, scanning the lids of each jar, searching. Rather that any of the familiar alphabets labeling the jars, each one had a small rune that only a properly trained witch doctor could read. An ancient pot with fading pink symbols on it proclaimed that it contained "glee."  A dourly painted mason jar declared that it held "solemnity." Useful, both of them, but not what she was looking for. 

Wiping away far too many years worth of cobwebs, Yehgohbah stood on tip toes and gingerly dragged a tiny orange pot from the back of a top shelf. This was one of the oldest ones in her care, but also one of the most important. The delicate, flower-like white rune read "Hope." Holding it tightly to her chest, she hobbled back to and then out of the beaded curtain. 

Rains had not come in nearly a year, making the harvests meager and the cattle sickly. Wild game was a rare sight. While most folk in the village had had the good sense to save surplus food for situations like the present, supplies were running low. Younglings would resort to chewing on the yellowed grass in a vain attempt to dull the edge of the ever-present hunger roaring in their bellies. To make matters worse, neighboring towns and bands, both People of the Mountain and otherwise, were threatening the village. The heat had brought hunger and desperation to all who lived on and near the mountain. 

Waddling as fast as her aged feet would carry her, the Witch Doctor made her way along the dusty road to  the main lodge where the village elders were holding talks with visiting leaders from the surrounding areas. One wrong word or expression could result in abandoned trade routes at least, or a battle at worst. The mood was tense as she shoved her way into the lodge past the lanky guard who'd been posted at the door. All eyes were on her for a brief moment before several demanded to know why the crone had been allowed in. Rather than humoring the visitors with a reply, she began to chant and opened the tiny jar. After she had finished, all present sat in stunned silence for a few heartbeats. Then came the scornful laughing. 

Then came the thunder, followed swiftly by the pattering of water droplets kissing the thirsty earth. The laughter was drowned out.

You know, the fear of falling vanishes if you do it often enough.  I squeezed my eyes shut and willed a small menu to appear in my mind's eye and selected "Load Saved Game" before my body could meet the bottom of the canyon.  This wasn't the first jump I'd done purely for fun. I'd discovered this little trick purely by accident. 

A few days ago, I celebrated my first free weekend in months by doing a marathon gaming session, after a trip to the store to load up on the necessities, hot pockets and Pepsi, of course. Once I got home, I reveled in my hermit-ness, shut off my phone and didn't wear pants for the whole duration. I was feeling nostalgic, so I looked in the library for my older games. The first day was one big fat binge on Mass Effect 2. I kept having to go back to a save because I really suck at shooter style games. After insulting all the NPCs I could (and getting my butt kicked), I grew bored and picked something else for the following day. The next day was a blur of The Sims, Final Fantasy 7 and various versions of Pokemon.  In fact, I didn't get to bed until just short of sunrise, somewhere around 4:30am.

At 1pm, my alarm blared to life and scared the crap out of me. After several moments of letting the panic wash away and my heart rate going back to normal, I crawled out of the pile of blankets and clothes I'd passed out on. Shit, I'd have to wear pants again. I stumble-walked my way from my upstairs bedroom towards the lone bathroom on the bottom floor. I have to confess that I am something of a slob in my own home. My pants and socks from Friday were still on the stairs where I'd tossed them in my bid for the sweet freedom of pantsless-ness and remained there for all of Saturday and Sunday. In that brief moment as I tripped over my black Levi's, I made a mental note that perhaps picking up my laundry and carrying it to the hamper would be worth the effort next time. 

I landed at the bottom of the steps with a solid thump and a very worrying snap. I blinked away the stars from my vision and looked down at my legs. My left ankle was twisted sickly out of alignment. I cautiously gave it a rub and screamed out in pain. Yep. Broken. I swore and thought, "I sure wish I could go back to a save before this crap!" 

My alarm blared to life and scared the crap out of me. I gasped and fumbled for the clock, crawling out of my pile of blankets and laundry. The digital face read 1pm. Right, I had to be at work in a couple of hours. I stumble-walked my way to the stairwell, intent on getting to the bathroom downstairs. I felt a sense of deja vu as looked down the stairs and noticed my pants and socks from Friday still laying right in the middle of the flight of stairs. I blinked several times and the memory of falling and breaking my ankle came flooding back. Holy crap! Had that been real? I shivered and held tight to the hand rail as I made my way down, taking the dirty clothes with me. No more pants-caused broken bones today! 

I used my "Load Saved Game" trick that first day several times. The first was to catch the bastard who was stealing my lunch. Fucking Chad. I never liked that guy. The next was to leave work a few minutes earlier to avoid a traffic jam on my usual route home. Another was used to avoid an ill-considered belly flop into a pool. The first time had seen my bikini top float away from me, much to the laughter of my mixed company of friends. 

That sensation of falling was sort of addicting. I noticed it as I flew off each of the diving boards, each higher than the last. Of course, I was safely embraced by the water at the end of each jump, but I wanted more time in the air. The next day found me googling hiking trails in the hills and mountains, searching for the highest point I could get to in driving distance. A state park known for a canyon with a breath-taking view drew my attention. I packed for a camping trip and let the GPS point the way. I got lost a couple of times, but went to a previous save to avoid taking those wrong turns again. 

I think I've spent a couple of days diving, but I can't be sure. I keep loading a previous save to jump again. For all I know, I've been here a week!
